title: Bend Their Reality
coreMove: Frame the choice around the loss, fairness standard, or anchor that changes how the deal feels.
sourcePressure: The source ties this chapter to fairness, loss aversion, anchoring, and perception, while warning that this is a high-risk abstraction zone that must stay concrete and not become careless manipulation.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must not drift into generic behavioral economics or make perception-shaping sound like a license to deceive.

hook: A casino table proves loss aversion
A car dealer anchors the buyer
People hate losing more than winning

exampleSpecs.domain: regional blood bank scheduling mobile drives
exampleSpecs.audience: a coordinator asking a corporate host to keep a low-turnout drive on the calendar
exampleSpecs.stakes: canceled appointments mean a hospital trauma unit starts the weekend short
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the coordinator reframes the request from adding inconvenience to preventing a specific platelet shortfall already scheduled for Friday
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cooler inventory screen showing two yellow platelet rows near zero

exampleSpecs.domain: hotel group-block dispute before a medical conference
exampleSpecs.audience: an event planner trying to keep a hotel from releasing reserved rooms
exampleSpecs.stakes: doctors may scatter across the city and miss early clinical sessions
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the planner uses the hotel's own service-standard language as the fairness reference point before discussing release dates
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a rooming-list spreadsheet open beside a brass key-card encoder

exampleSpecs.domain: print shop rush order for election ballots
exampleSpecs.audience: a county clerk negotiating with a printer after a proofing error
exampleSpecs.stakes: late ballots could force public notice and erode trust in the election process
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the clerk anchors on the public cost of a missed mailing date rather than the shop's overtime charge
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a proof sheet with one precinct line circled in red pencil

exampleSpecs.audience: a project lead asking a church board to sign after the rebate changed
exampleSpecs.stakes: the board may walk away if the new price feels like a bait and switch
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the lead stops defending the higher monthly number and reframes the loss as forfeiting locked winter credits already reserved in the church's name
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a utility bill with the winter credit line highlighted beside a chapel floor plan

exampleSpecs.domain: specialty tool rental dispute after storm damage
exampleSpecs.audience: a rental manager negotiating with a contractor who resists the damage charge
exampleSpecs.stakes: the contractor may walk from a long account if the charge feels arbitrary
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager frames the charge against the signed replacement schedule and asks what would feel fair given the cracked torque housing in front of them
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cracked torque housing resting on a black rubber service mat

exampleSpecs.audience: an editor discussing royalty terms with a narrator after production delays
exampleSpecs.stakes: the audiobook may miss a seasonal launch if both sides lock onto hourly rate
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the editor reviews how shifting from hourly loss to launch-window upside changed the narrator's perception of a revised royalty split
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a waveform timeline paused at chapter eight on a studio monitor

skillTargets: identify whether a frame uses loss, fairness, or anchor pressure
apply a concrete fairness reference without manipulation
analyze how a reference point changes perceived value
evaluate when perception-shaping crosses into careless distortion

tryThisNowSpec: For one stalled offer, write the number, then write the loss or fairness standard the other side is using to judge that number; revise your next sentence around that reference point.
sourceAnchorsNote: source contains no named anecdote for this chapter

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: prevents the timestamp+named-protagonist template from dominating the chapter

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following 'concrete anchor -> abstract rule -> elaboration'
